title: Configuration
text: Every environment variable an operator needs, and which ones are hard-required. PayOS is 12-factor: everything the services read is an environment variable, and nothing secret is ever committed. Locally, the compose stack ships with safe dev defaults; for a real deployment you set these yourself (via your cloud's secret store — see Deploy to the Cloud). This page covers the variables an operator cares about. You do not need to touch most of them locally — the defaults just work.

title: Core service configuration
text: Variable Read by Purpose --- --- --- ✱ server + worker Postgres — the system of record and the job queue. server Cache / rate-limit only. Correctness survives a Redis flush; the worker reads no Redis. ✱ (+ , …) server + worker Versioned AES-256-GCM keys that seal provider credentials at rest. 32 bytes hex (64 hex chars). The highest suffix is the active key; lower versions still open older data (that's how rotation works). Must be byte-identical on server and worker. ✱ server + worker The secret the licensing engine keys license-key lookups under. Identical on both. Generate with . server 32-byte (64 hex) seed for the Ed25519 offline-grace receipt key. Set it in production so cached receipts keep verifying across restarts; omit it and the server generates one per boot (fine for a single dev box). ✱ server The API's public base URL, reachable from browsers and providers. server + worker Hosted-pages base — checkout success/cancel URLs, portal links in emails. server + worker Dashboard base — the onboarding link and OAuth callbacks. the 3 apps The internal origin the Next.js apps proxy to — their only backend config. server in production (HTTPS); only for plain-http local dev. / server When both are set, the platform admin is upserted at startup (password hashed, never logged). ✱ = hard-required — the binary refuses to start without it. The compose stack uses fixed throwaway values for , , , and the admin/vendor passwords so that a fresh just works. Generate your own for any non-local deployment ( ), and store them in your cloud's secret store — never in git.

title: Connecting payment providers (platform level)
text: Most providers are connected by the vendor in the dashboard and need no platform config. Four providers support one-click OAuth, which the platform operator enables once per deployment by setting both halves of a credential pair: Provider Variables (set both) --- --- Stripe + PayPal + Square + Mollie + With both set, the dashboard shows a "Connect with …" button. With either missing, that provider falls back to the manual key wizard (a half-configured pair is ignored with a startup warning). Every other provider — Coinbase Commerce, Paddle, Braintree, Adyen, Authorize.net, Lemon Squeezy, NOWPayments, and BTCPay — uses the guided manual wizard and needs no platform variables.

title: Deploy to the Cloud
text: Deploy the same container images to Railway, AWS, GCP, or DigitalOcean with one command. PayOS deploys the same container images the local compose stack runs — to Railway, AWS, GCP, or DigitalOcean — with one command: Under the hood this wraps . Every target runs the identical five images ( , , , , ). Migrations run automatically at startup behind a Postgres advisory lock — there is no separate migration step on any cloud. A real / needs your own cloud account and credentials. What ships is validated to the credential boundary: build a sane resource graph, the scripts are idempotent, and fails loudly (rather than half-deploying) when credentials are missing. The actual multi-cloud apply is the operator's step once accounts exist — the same posture as certifying a real payment provider.

text: === "AWS" Needs the AWS CLI authenticated and an ACM certificate ARN for the HTTPS listener. Uses the account default VPC unless / are set. Point the api/dashboard/web/pages DNS records at the ALB output. === "GCP" Needs authenticated on the target . Map custom domains onto the Cloud Run URLs to match the values. === "DigitalOcean" The reference is an all-in-one App Platform app. For strict per-hostname routing, the recommended production topology is one app per frontend sharing the managed Postgres, Redis, and DOCR. === "Railway" Railway is CLI/config-driven (not Terraform). title: Idempotency & safety
text: Re-running converges — Terraform reconciles to declared state; re-rolls. Fail-loud — missing credentials, an unauthenticated Railway CLI, or a tracked all abort with a clear message, never a silent partial deploy. No committed secrets — only placeholders are tracked.

The fast path: get the whole PayOS stack running locally and drive a real purchase end-to-end — no payment provider account required. Budget a couple of minutes plus the first image build.

title: Using PayOS — For Customers
text: Buying, license keys, and the self-service magic-link portal. You're buying a product from a vendor who uses PayOS. This is what that looks like, and how to manage what you bought afterward. Everything is vendor-branded — you see the vendor's name, logo, and colors, not PayOS's.

title: Buying
text: 1. From the vendor's website you land on a hosted pricing page (something like ). Pick the plan you want and click Buy. 2. On the checkout page, enter your email and choose a payment method — whichever the vendor enabled: card, PayPal, a wallet (Apple Pay / Google Pay), or crypto. 3. Complete payment on the provider's own secure hosted page. PayOS never sees or stores your card details. 4. You're returned to a completion page.

title: If you bought a licensed product
text: The completion page shows your license key, and it's also emailed to you. Copy it and paste it into the product to activate. Each key can run on a limited number of machines (set by the vendor).

title: If you bought a subscription
text: Your subscription is active immediately; you'll be billed each period until you cancel. You'll receive a receipt by email for every payment.

title: Managing your purchases: the portal
text: The vendor gives you a self-service portal — no password to remember. Sign in with a magic link: 1. Go to the vendor's portal page (something like ). 2. Enter your email and submit. Check your inbox for a sign-in link. 3. Click the link. You're in — the link is single-use and expires in 15 minutes, and your session lasts about a week. The portal shows the same "check your inbox" message no matter what — it never reveals whether an email has an account. Only a real buyer's inbox gets a link. Inside the portal you can:

title: View purchases and receipts
text: See everything you've bought from this vendor, with a receipt for each payment.

title: Reveal and copy license keys
text: Each license shows masked ( ) with a Reveal button. Click it to show the full key and copy it. (Reveal is rate-limited — copy it when you reveal it.)

title: Manage your machines ("I got a new laptop")
text: Each license lists the machines it's active on. If you've hit the machine limit and need to move to a new device, Deactivate an old machine — that frees a slot immediately so the new machine can activate. No support ticket needed.

title: Cancel a subscription
text: Open the subscription and click Cancel. It's set to cancel at the end of the current period — you keep access until then, and you won't be billed again.

title: Sign out
text: Use Sign out to end your session. Sign back in any time with a new magic link.

title: Good to know
text: Your data is scoped to this vendor — a portal for vendor A never shows anything from vendor B. If your session expires, the portal simply asks you to sign in again with a fresh magic link. Already-purchased license keys keep working even if the vendor's account has a billing issue — your purchase is yours.

title: Using PayOS — For Platform Admins
text: Onboard vendors, mint tokens, and watch platform health. The platform admin operates PayOS itself: onboarding vendors, suspending and reinstating them, and watching platform health. Admins work in the super-admin console, which lives in the app. URL (local): http://localhost:3002 Sign in: / (dev seed — change for production) The admin plane is cross-tenant and completely separate from any vendor's dashboard: a vendor login can never reach it, and an admin session is never scoped to a single tenant.

title: Onboard a new vendor
text: Vendor signup is invitation-only — a vendor account can only be created by redeeming a single-use onboarding token. There are two ways a token is minted.

title: The dogfood path (automatic)
text: PayOS sells itself. When someone buys PayOS Lifetime or PayOS Monthly through PayOS's own checkout, the system automatically mints an onboarding token, emails it to the buyer, and the buyer redeems it to create their vendor account. No admin action required — this is the self-serve growth loop.

title: The sales/ops path (you mint it)
text: To onboard a vendor directly: 1. In the super-admin console, open Onboarding tokens and choose Mint token. 2. Optionally bind it to an email (so only that address can redeem it) and set an expiry (1–365 days, default 30). 3. The raw token is shown exactly once — copy it now. PayOS stores only a hash; the listing afterward never shows the token again. 4. Send the token (or the signup link that carries it) to your new vendor. The vendor then redeems it at the dashboard's page (the token is prefilled from the link). They enter a vendor name, email, and password, and their account — vendor + owner user — is created atomically and logged in.

title: Suspend or reinstate a vendor
text: Use this for a delinquent or misbehaving vendor. On the Vendors view, each vendor has a Suspend / Reinstate button. What suspension does — without ever punishing buyers who already paid: Plane While suspended --- --- Hosted pricing/checkout pages Go dark — products read as unavailable. New checkouts Refused before anything is charged. API-key / query plane Returns . Vendor dashboard Drops into read-only mode — the vendor can still view everything (analytics, payments, settings) but cannot make changes. What keeps working: a suspended vendor's already-sold license keys keep validating and activating machines. A buyer is only ever blocked by their own license being revoked, never by the vendor's status. This is a hard guarantee. Reinstate flips the vendor back to active and their pages come back on the next request. Every suspend/reinstate is recorded in the append-only audit log.

title: Automated dunning (PayOS's own billing)
text: Vendors who pay for PayOS monthly are subject to automatic dunning if their own PayOS subscription goes past-due: Three reminder emails are sent (on day 0, day 7, and day 12). On day 14, the vendor is auto-suspended — recorded with a actor and a cause, distinct from a manual admin suspension. If the vendor pays up, a subscription renewal auto-reinstates them (this only lifts a dunning suspension, never an unrelated admin one). A vendor on the one-time (lifetime) plan is never subject to dunning.

title: View platform health and attention items
text: The console surfaces the platform's overall state — vendors and their statuses, onboarding tokens outstanding, and the items that need attention (delinquent vendors, for example). Because PayOS is its own Vendor #0, its own billing status shows up here too.

title: Where to go next
text: Hand your new vendor the Vendor guide so they can connect providers and create products. Operators configuring the platform: Configuration.

title: Using PayOS — For Vendors
text: Connect providers, create products, and manage licensing from the vendor dashboard. You're a vendor: you sell products and want PayOS to handle pricing, checkout, providers, licensing, and your customer portal. Everything you do lives in the vendor dashboard. URL (local): http://localhost:3001 Demo sign-in: / Everything below applies per environment — a test side for rehearsal and a live side for real money. Test data never bleeds into live listings or analytics. Switch environments with the control in the dashboard.

title: 1. Sign up (redeem your onboarding token)
text: You need an onboarding token — either emailed to you automatically after buying PayOS, or minted for you by a platform admin (see For Platform Admins). 1. Open the signup link ( ) — the token is prefilled. Or go to the dashboard's Sign up page and paste the token. 2. Enter your vendor name, a slug (this becomes part of your public page URLs, e.g. ), your email, and a password. 3. Submit. Your vendor account and owner login are created and you're signed in.

title: 2. Connect a payment provider
text: You bring your own provider accounts — money flows straight to you. Open Providers and pick one. There are two connect styles:

title: One-click OAuth (Stripe, PayPal, Square, Mollie)
text: If the platform operator has enabled it, you'll see a "Connect with …" button. Click it, complete the provider's own hosted flow (which handles account creation, KYC, and bank details), and the credentials return to PayOS automatically. You never touch an API key.

title: Guided manual setup (everyone else)
text: Coinbase Commerce, Paddle, Braintree, Adyen, Authorize.net, Lemon Squeezy, NOWPayments, and self-hosted BTCPay use a step-by-step wizard: it links you to the provider's signup, tells you exactly where to find each key, you paste them in, and PayOS validates the credentials server-side before saving. The per-provider steps are documented in detail in the engineering provider pages (serve them with ). Connecting a live provider requires that provider's own merchant/sandbox account — that's expected. To learn the flows first, the demo vendor ships with a built-in mock provider so you can complete checkouts with no real account. You can connect multiple providers, and choose which ones a given product offers. A crypto provider is one-time-only (it can't back subscriptions).

title: 3. Create a product, plans, and prices
text: Open Products → New product. A product is either: One-time — a single purchase. Gets an implicit plan; you just set prices. Can have licensing enabled (see below). Subscription — recurring. You add explicit plans (e.g. Monthly, Yearly), each with a billing interval and optional trial days. Then: 1. Give it a name, slug, and description. (The slug is permanent — it's baked into your public URLs.) 2. Add at least one price. Prices are in a currency (ISO code) and integer minor units (e.g. = $25.00). Prices are append-only — changing a price archives the old one so historical sales keep their original price. 3. For a subscription, add your plans and a price on each.

title: Licensing config (one-time products only)
text: While the product is still a draft, set: Licensing enabled — issue a license key on each confirmed payment. Max machines — how many machines one key may activate. Revalidation days — how often the customer's software should re-check online. These lock once the product goes active (sold keys copy the values at issuance), so get them right first.

title: Activate it
text: A product must pass a readiness gate before going live — it needs a name, a description, and at least one active price on an active plan. Flip it from draft → active and it's buyable. (You can archive a product later; archiving freezes it and its plans/prices but keeps reads working.)

title: 4. Choose providers per product & set branding
text: Providers per product: enable which connected providers a product offers at checkout. Buyers see exactly those methods. Branding: set a logo, banner, and accent color on the product; the hosted pricing/checkout page and the customer portal render with them. Theme: pick from the 7 built-in themes with the switcher at the top-right — it applies consistently across the surfaces. Your product's public page is now live at — link to it from your website. That link is your entire integration.

title: 5. Issue refunds
text: On the Payments view, open a payment and choose Refund (full or partial, where the provider supports it). PayOS calls the provider and records the refund; if licensing is enabled, a full refund revokes the license automatically. PayOS also observes refunds you make directly in a provider's own dashboard and reconciles them into its ledger, so your numbers stay honest either way.

title: 6. Developer settings: webhooks & API keys
text: Under Developer settings, wire your own backend to PayOS: Outbound webhooks — register an HTTPS endpoint and PayOS POSTs signed events to it the moment they happen: , , , , , , and more. Verify the HMAC on the raw body, respond to acknowledge, and make your handler idempotent. You can rotate the signing secret. API keys — create scoped keys ( / ), shown once at creation. Use them for the query API: create checkouts, read subscriptions and licenses, check a customer's entitlement, or revoke a license. Scope each key to only what it needs. The pattern: a webhook tells your backend "something happened, here are the ids"; your handler then calls the query API for full detail. Never trust a browser redirect as proof of payment — confirm server-side.

title: 7. Read your analytics
text: The Analytics view answers "how is my business doing?" Pick an environment, a date range, and a grouping: Summary (KPIs): revenue per currency (gross / refunded / net), payment count, active subscribers, refund rate, and new/total customers. Revenue series: grouped by time (day/week/month), country, product, or provider. Subscribers: active count, new, churned, and MRR per currency. A few honest notes: money is never summed across currencies (you get a line per currency), and MRR counts monthly-interval subscriptions only — treat it as a monthly run-rate, not a GAAP figure. Analytics keep working even while a vendor is suspended (reads are always allowed).

title: 8. Invite your team
text: Under Team, invite other users to your vendor account. Roles are and ; the last owner can't be removed, so an account always has one.

title: Test vs live, in practice
text: Do everything on test first — connect a test/mock provider, create a product, run a checkout, watch the webhook fire and the analytics update. When it all works, switch to live, connect your real provider, and repeat. The two are fully isolated.
